details:
**Contact process**
The modern industrial method for making sulfuric acid. Sulfur dioxide is oxidized to sulfur trioxide over a vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) catalyst at about 450 °C and 1–2 atm. The SO3 is absorbed into concentrated sulfuric acid to make oleum, which is then diluted with water. Vanadium oxide replaced platinum, which was poisoned by arsenic impurities.

**Lead chamber process**
The older, now obsolete way to make sulfuric acid. It was developed by John Roebuck, who used large lead-lined chambers. Nitrogen oxides catalyze the oxidation of sulfur dioxide. The Gay-Lussac tower recovers the nitrogen oxides and the Glover tower returns them to the system while concentrating the acid.

**Lead-acid batteries**
Car batteries use dilute sulfuric acid as the electrolyte between lead and lead dioxide plates. Discharging turns both plates into lead sulfate and uses up the acid; recharging re-forms the sulfuric acid. Gaston Planté's lead-acid cell was the first rechargeable battery.

**Only diprotic strong acid**
Sulfuric acid can give up two protons, and its first dissociation is complete in water, so it is the classic example of a strong diprotic acid. Sulfur in it has a +6 oxidation state. It is the most produced industrial chemical in the world.

**Oleum (fuming sulfuric acid)**
A solution of sulfur trioxide in sulfuric acid, also written as disulfuric (pyrosulfuric) acid, H2S2O7. It forms as an intermediate step in the contact process and is diluted with water to give concentrated sulfuric acid.

**Oil of vitriol**
The historical, alchemical name for sulfuric acid. It was once made by the dry distillation of "vitriols" (metal sulfates) or of pyrite. Johann Glauber also made it by burning sulfur with steam (saltpeter).

**Dehydration of sugar (carbon snake)**
Concentrated sulfuric acid is a strong dehydrating agent. Poured on sucrose, it pulls out the water and leaves a rising black column of carbon, a popular chemistry demonstration. It chars cotton and other carbohydrates in the same way.

**Jones reagent**
Chromium trioxide dissolved in aqueous sulfuric acid, usually added to an acetone solution of the substrate. It oxidizes primary alcohols to carboxylic acids and secondary alcohols to ketones.

**Hammett acidity function of about −12 and superacids**
Pure sulfuric acid has a Hammett acidity function (H0) of about −12. A superacid is defined as any acid stronger than 100% sulfuric acid; magic acid, for example, has an H0 of about −23.

**Nitration of benzene (nitrating mixture)**
In electrophilic aromatic nitration, sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to form the nitronium ion (NO2+), the electrophile that attacks benzene. Heating an aromatic compound in sulfuric acid also sulfonates it, which can be used to block the para position.

**Leblanc and Mannheim processes**
In the first step of the Leblanc process for making sodium carbonate, sulfuric acid reacts with sodium chloride to form sodium sulfate (salt cake) and hydrogen chloride. The Mannheim process uses the same reaction to make sodium sulfate and hydrochloric acid.

**Wet process for phosphoric acid**
Sulfuric acid's main use is treating phosphate rock (apatite or fluorapatite) to make phosphoric acid and phosphate fertilizers, which makes the phosphates easier for plants to take up. The byproduct is gypsum.

**Acid rain and the clouds of Venus**
Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels oxidizes in the atmosphere and reacts with water to form sulfuric acid, a major part of acid rain. Venus's thick clouds are made of sulfuric acid droplets, and sulfuric acid is also proposed to exist on Europa.

**Bunsen reaction (sulfur–iodine cycle)**
Sulfur dioxide, iodine, and water react to form sulfuric acid and hydrogen iodide. This is a key step in the sulfur–iodine thermochemical cycle, which splits water to make hydrogen.

**Wet sulfuric acid (WSA) process and DCDA**
The WSA process, developed by the Danish company Haldor Topsøe, makes sulfuric acid from wet sulfur-containing gases. DCDA (double contact, double absorption) is a version of the contact process that absorbs SO3 twice to raise yield and cut emissions.
